item.question: Proposed question: Does the build use machine-state lifecycle operations - pause, resume, and fork of a paused sandbox - where the isolation class offers them, and is it free of the errors the window has ruled out?
item.target: Suspension, resumption and forking are capability operations with a defined answer when an adapter cannot serve them, and the security boundary chosen for untrusted output is not a shared kernel.

closures.mechanism: A mature build treats pause, resume and fork of a sandbox as capability operations on the isolation adapter, not ad hoc scripting: pausing checkpoints the sandbox's memory and filesystem state (a microVM snapshot, or an equivalent CRIU-based checkpoint), resume restores from that snapshot in tens of milliseconds, and fork clones a paused or running sandbox from a shared base without re-provisioning. Where the underlying adapter cannot serve one of these operations, the interface returns a defined, typed unsupported result rather than silently degrading or emulating it. The security boundary chosen for untrusted output is a dedicated guest kernel (a microVM such as Firecracker) or an intercepting user-space kernel (gVisor) -- never a shared host kernel, which several 2026 sandbox-escape incidents show is the boundary attackers actually cross.
closures.standard: none -- no standards body governs sandbox lifecycle operations; the OCI Runtime Spec covers container configuration but not pause/resume/fork semantics, so this is vendor convention (Firecracker snapshot-restore, CRIU) rather than a ratified spec.
closures.check: a state-hash test: snapshot a running sandbox, compute a digest of memory+filesystem state, resume it, and assert the digest is unchanged before any further syscall; separately, a conformance test that calls fork on an adapter lacking the operation and asserts a typed unsupported error rather than a crash or silent no-op.
closures.direction: Settling: checkpoint/restore is becoming table stakes across providers (E2B, Daytona, Fly Sprites, Runloop, Vercel, CodeSandbox all shipped some form by mid-2026), and microVMs vs. gVisor is a live, deliberate tradeoff (isolation strength vs. cold-start cost), not a settled winner. Being abandoned: sharing a host kernel between the agent's untrusted output and the host as the isolation boundary.
closures.quote: Firecracker's snapshot-restore mechanism lets you pause a sandbox, preserve its memory and filesystem state, and resume it in 5-30ms.

item.question: Proposed: Is the production of the failure object owned by one place the core imports, so a new capability adapter cannot invent its own failure shape?
item.target: Adapters raise typed conditions that the shared construction point renders; there is no second place a failure body is built.

closures.mechanism: A mature build owns problem-object construction at exactly one place the core imports -- a shared error-rendering component (e.g. a global exception handler / controller-advice-equivalent) -- and every capability adapter raises a typed condition into it rather than building a problem+json body itself. The shared point is the only place that knows how to serialize the standard fields (type, title, status, detail, instance) plus any extension members, so adding a new adapter means defining a new typed condition, never a new serialization path.
closures.standard: RFC 9457, Problem Details for HTTP APIs (RFC Editor, July 2023, obsoletes RFC 7807) -- baseline, no credible competitor for the wire shape; centralization of its construction is framework convention layered on top, not part of the RFC itself.
closures.check: a source scan asserting exactly one code path constructs the problem-detail/content-type object (e.g. one class or module owns `application/problem+json` serialization); a test that raises every typed condition the build defines and asserts each is rendered by that same single path, never a second one.
closures.direction: Settling: recent framework majors (e.g. Spring Boot 4) make centralized, framework-wide Problem Details handling the default with no per-controller opt-in, confirming the direction toward one shared rendering point. Nothing in the window is displacing RFC 9457 itself as the wire format.
closures.quote: In Spring Boot 4, unified framework-wide error handling with Problem Details is now a standard, allowing centralized handling that no longer requires manual opt-in for every controller.

item.question: Can it be shown that no artifact escapes the guarantee, that every artifact produced over a period has a record, and that a component cannot produce one through a path which emits nothing? (This question is proposed, derived from the row it cites.)
item.target: The two counts reconcile with no unattested artifact; emission is wired where every producing path passes, so a component that attests nothing itself still yields a record; the attempt to write outside that path is refused or is structurally impossible.

closures.mechanism: A mature build wires attestation emission into the one execution boundary every artifact-producing action must pass through, so a component that itself calls no attestation API still yields a record -- emission is a property of the path, not of the producer's cooperation. A reconciliation job counts artifacts produced against attestations issued for the same period and treats any mismatch as a defect; the attempt to write an artifact outside the wired path is refused by the platform (e.g. no credential to publish through any other route) rather than merely discouraged by convention. Because an attestation alone is only a linkage claim, the guarantee is enforced a second time at deployment/consumption via admission policy that refuses anything unattested.
closures.standard: in-toto Attestation Framework plus SLSA provenance (build platform attests at Level 2+ with signed provenance); no single standard mandates the coverage guarantee itself, which is implemented as pipeline and admission-policy design.
closures.check: a count reconciliation: number of artifacts recorded in the artifact store equals the number of valid, matching attestations issued in the same window, enforced by an admission-time policy check (e.g. a ValidatingImagePolicy-equivalent) that structurally refuses any artifact without one.
closures.direction: Settling: attestation generation is moving from opt-in to default for public/production pipelines through 2025-2026, and enforcement is moving from "attestation exists" to "attestation is evaluated at admission time," since attestations alone were shown not to guarantee security by themselves.
closures.quote: for public repositories, attestation generation is shifting from opt-in to default behavior

item.evidence: harness/provenance/conformance.py VERIFIER constant, the string a caller sees as external_verifier in every conformance report: "(written in this repository; a verifier we did not write is not available here)", following the path harness/provenance/conformance.py --verify-bundle, run as a separate p

closures.mechanism: A mature build verifies its own provenance/attestation claims with a verifier that shares no codebase or authorship with the system under verification -- an externally maintained, widely used tool run as a separate process against the signed statement and a trust root the verifier does not itself issue. Where no such external verifier is wired in yet, the honest state is to say so explicitly in the conformance output (naming the gap) rather than to substitute a verifier written inside the repository being verified, which cannot prove independence of the claim it is checking.

closures.direction: Settling: cosign/Sigstore's keyless, trusted-root verification is the practical default external verifier for in-toto-shaped attestations; the in-toto project's own prototype verifier is explicitly marked unfit for production, reinforcing that an in-repo or reference verifier is not a substitute for an external one. This is a genuine gap this platform has (VERIFIER: "a verifier we did not write is not available here"), not a difference of philosophy.

item.evidence: docs/decomposition.md records the search as issued queries, and records the one fetch attempt failing: "returned `EGRESS_BLOCKED` from the network egress proxy". kb/research.jsonl holds 660 research records; I counted status and read fields with python3 (json load over the file): 660 of 660 are stat

closures.mechanism: A mature build enforces default-deny network egress for any sandbox doing research or executing agent-directed code, routed through a proxy the agent cannot bypass, with a narrow allowlist for the hosts a given task actually needs; every blocked attempt is itself written as a typed record (not dropped silently), so a downstream count of research citations can be reconciled against the proxy's own access log. When a fetch is blocked, the mature response is to route the same request through a permitted path (an allowlisted search/fetch tool) and record the substitution, rather than leave a claim uncorroborated by a live fetch.
closures.standard: none formally normative -- egress control for agent sandboxes is an emerging best-practice pattern (default-deny proxy allowlisting), not governed by a standards body; vendor-specific allowlist configuration mechanisms exist.
closures.check: reconcile the proxy's access-decision log against the research-record file: every URL cited with status "search-only" has a matching allow decision in the log, and every EGRESS_BLOCKED event has a corresponding record rather than being silently dropped.
closures.direction: Settling: default-deny egress at an unavoidable proxy is treated as the single highest-leverage agent-security control, and disclosed 2026 sandbox-escape incidents that exploited proxy vulnerabilities to gain unrestricted egress are reinforcing that direction, not weakening it. EGRESS_BLOCKED as a broad, sometimes over-aggressive failure mode is a known current pain point across tooling, not unique to this platform.
closures.quote: Default-deny egress at a proxy the agent cannot route around is the highest-leverage single control for agent security.

item.claim: Which isolation class operators running hundreds of concurrent agent units actually default to, with measured cost per resident sandbox.
item.research_query: operators running hundreds of concurrent agent sandboxes 2026 default isolation class measured cost per resident sandbox

closures.mechanism: Operators running large fleets of concurrent agent sandboxes do not pick one isolation class uniformly: gVisor's user-space kernel is the default for cost-sensitive, high-concurrency, trusted-enough workloads (one major operator names 20,000+ concurrent gVisor-isolated containers and 50,000+ concurrent sandboxed sessions), while microVMs (Firecracker-class, dedicated guest kernel) are reserved for workloads needing the stronger isolation boundary against untrusted agent-generated code, at a measured per-vCPU-hour/GB-hour cost. Past a measured volume threshold, operators shift from a managed sandbox provider to self-hosting the microVM layer because the unit economics cross over.
closures.standard: none -- no standard sets a default isolation class; the OCI Runtime Spec defines the interface, not the choice of implementation.
closures.check: a per-resident-sandbox cost dashboard (actual vCPU-hr + GiB-hr billed per second) reconciled monthly against the measured self-host crossover point (roughly 500 sandbox-hours/month in one measured case), driving an explicit build-vs-buy decision at that line rather than a fixed policy.
closures.direction: Settling: gVisor as the higher-concurrency, lower-cost default with microVMs reserved for stronger isolation needs; self-hosting the microVM layer once volume clears a measured hundreds-of-sandbox-hours-per-month threshold. Being abandoned: plain shared-kernel containers as the isolation boundary for untrusted, agent-generated code.
closures.quote: Self-hosting the Firecracker layer cuts per-execution cost 60-80% once you clear roughly 500 sandbox-hours a month.
closures.gap: the exact measured cost per resident sandbox specifically at a "hundreds of concurrent agents" scale (as opposed to the thousands/tens-of-thousands figures the search surfaced) was not isolated in any single source; the $0.017/vCPU-hr and $0.008/GB-hr managed-provider figures and the 500-sandbox-hour self-host crossover are the closest measured data points found. Query used: "operators running hundreds of concurrent agent sandboxes 2026 default isolation class measured cost per resident sandbox".

item.claim: That any cross-engine specification or portable journal format for durable execution exists or is being drafted inside the window.
item.research_query: cross-engine durable execution specification portable workflow journal format working group 2026

closures.mechanism: A mature build treats durable execution as a journal of completed execution boundaries -- tool calls, external mutations, human approvals, outbound messages -- persisted before their result is returned to the calling function, so a crash recovers by replaying the journal without repeating any side effect. No cross-engine specification or portable journal wire format exists inside the window (each engine journals in its own format: Temporal's history, Restate's journal, DBOS's Postgres-backed log), so portability is achieved tool-agnostically at the capability interface -- a build codes to the durable-execution contract, keeping any given engine's journal format an internal implementation detail, so a second engine can be substituted behind that interface without the format itself needing to be shared.
closures.standard: none -- durable execution as a category is settling (Temporal, Restate, DBOS and others converging on the journal-before-return mechanism), but no cross-engine journal-format standard or working group was found in the window; one academic proposal names a five-plane interoperability taxonomy without a ratified spec.
closures.check: a resume test: kill the process mid-workflow at a marked step and assert the resumed run neither repeats the completed side effect nor loses state -- validated per-engine against its own journal, since no cross-engine assertion is currently possible.
closures.direction: Emerging: cross-language client interoperability within one engine (DBOS shipped multi-language clients against one workflow in April 2026) is happening; a shared cross-engine journal format is not. Abandoned: expecting one canonical durable-execution wire format to emerge and be adopted across engines inside this window.
closures.quote: A durable execution engine works by journaling progress as code runs, with every meaningful step recorded to a persistent log before its result is returned to the function.
closures.gap: no cross-engine durable-execution journal specification or working group was found; only single-vendor cross-language interoperability (DBOS) surfaced. Query used: "cross-engine durable execution specification portable workflow journal format working group 2026".

item.claim: Whether a conformance test suite published by the protocol's stewards exists that an adapter can be run against.
item.research_query: Agent Client Protocol official conformance test suite certification 2026

closures.mechanism: A mature agent protocol's stewards publish an official, steward-authored conformance test suite -- a reference client and/or server pair that any implementation runs against for certification, ideally on a re-validation cadence tied to protocol versions -- so conformance is a mechanical, third-party-verifiable claim rather than a self-report. Where stewards have not yet published one, the interim, weaker substitute is a community-built inspector/validator that checks wire traffic against the published schema, which catches structural non-conformance but cannot certify behavioral conformance the way a steward-authored suite can.
closures.standard: Agent Client Protocol (agentclientprotocol.com / github.com/agentclientprotocol), an open protocol for connecting editors to coding agents; no version-specific conformance-suite normative text was found.
closures.check: none official exists for ACP; the closest mechanical check available is running an implementation's traffic through a third-party inspector (e.g. acp-inspector) for schema-conformance validation -- not a certification against a steward-defined pass/fail suite.
closures.direction: Emerging: the adjacent MCP ecosystem shipped an official, steward-authored conformance-test repository in 2026, setting the expected pattern for agent protocols generally; ACP's stewards have not followed with an equivalent suite in this window, leaving only third-party tooling.
closures.quote: ACP Inspector is a tool for debugging and validating Agent Client Protocol (ACP) traffic through protocol conformance testing for AI coding agents
closures.gap: no steward-published, official ACP conformance test suite was found; only third-party community inspector/validator tools (ACP-inspector, acp-inspector) exist, which check spec-schema conformance of traffic but are not an official certification suite. Query used: "Agent Client Protocol official conformance test suite certification 2026".

item.claim: Whether the packaging specification itself defines a version field, a digest or a signature mechanism, as opposed to registries and runtimes adding these around it.
item.research_query: Agent Skills specification manifest fields version integrity digest signature normative requirements 2026

closures.mechanism: The base packaging specification for a portable skill/capability defines only the minimal manifest needed for discovery and instruction (in the Agent Skills spec's case: YAML frontmatter with name and description, plus a Markdown body) and leaves version, digest and signature as non-normative additions. Where integrity matters, a mature ecosystem layers a signing mechanism around the base spec rather than waiting for the spec itself to grow one -- a root certificate plus a verifier tool (e.g. an external, OpenSSF-aligned model-signing verifier) covering every file in the package -- while a v1 packaging spec may explicitly defer the trust decision to install-time human review instead of a cryptographic layer.
closures.standard: Agent Skills specification v1 (agentskills.io, originated by Anthropic, published as an open standard 2025-12-18) -- normative surface is two required frontmatter fields plus a Markdown body; no normative digest or signature mechanism.
closures.check: a schema check confirming SKILL.md frontmatter contains only the spec-required fields (name, description) and that any version/digest/signature field present is a vendor extension, cross-checked against whether the package is separately signed by an external verifier (e.g. an OpenSSF Model Signing check) rather than the manifest schema enforcing integrity itself.
closures.direction: Settling: third-party signing layers (root certificate plus an external verifier) are being bolted onto the unsigned base spec rather than the base spec itself growing a normative integrity layer inside the window; a closely related packaging spec (Agent Plugins 1.0) explicitly chose install-time human review over a signing layer for v1. Abandoned: waiting for the Agent Skills spec itself to define version/digest/signature fields before shipping integrity tooling.
closures.quote: Version 1 defines no provenance or permissions layer, and no signing layer either -- the trust decision moves entirely to your install-time review

item.claim: Whether the agent messaging standard's extension mechanism is in practice used to carry idempotency keys and budget ceilings, or whether implementers put them in the payload.
item.research_query: A2A extension mechanism 1.0.1 examples idempotency key budget metadata extension registry usage 2026

closures.mechanism: A2A's extension mechanism is used in practice for cross-cutting concerns generally -- an agent declares support for an extension as an AgentExtension entry in its AgentCard, a caller activates it via the A2A-Extensions request header, and extension-specific data rides in the message's arbitrary key-value metadata keyed by the extension's URI. Idempotency itself is handled today mostly through the base spec's own messageId-based duplicate detection rather than through a dedicated extension; a normative idempotency-key extension (A2A-SAGA) exists only as an open community proposal, and no budget-ceiling extension of any kind was found, official or proposed.
closures.standard: Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol, contributed to the Linux Foundation in 2026; the extension mechanism (AgentCard AgentExtension objects, A2A-Extensions header, metadata) is part of the core specification, but no specific extension for idempotency keys or budget ceilings has been ratified.
closures.check: scan an AgentCard's declared capabilities for an AgentExtension URI in a recognized idempotency/budget namespace, cross-checked against actual A2A-Extensions header usage on requests -- expected to return none for most implementers today, since no official extension exists yet.
closures.direction: Emerging: the extension mechanism itself is settled and actively used for other concerns (tracing, credential passports); idempotency-key and budget-ceiling usage specifically remains at the community-proposal stage inside this window, with implementers more likely to rely on the base spec's messageId field or put such data directly in the message payload.
closures.quote: The A2A-SAGA extension introduces normative requirements for idempotency_key propagation to ensure safe retries.
closures.gap: no ratified or widely-implemented A2A extension for idempotency keys or budget ceilings was found; only a community discussion/proposal (A2A-SAGA, GitHub discussion #1324) surfaced for idempotency_key, and nothing at all for budget metadata specifically. Query used: "A2A extension mechanism 1.0.1 examples idempotency key budget metadata extension registry usage 2026".

item.claim: Whether the CloudEvents distributed-tracing extension and explicit correlation attributes are used together in practice, or whether implementers choose one and lose the other.
item.research_query: CloudEvents distributed tracing extension plus explicit correlation attributes agent workflow 2026 implementation guidance conflict

closures.mechanism: A mature build carries both together, because they serve different jobs rather than competing: the CloudEvents distributed-tracing extension embeds a W3C Trace Context traceparent/tracestate pair for cross-system trace correlation with OpenTelemetry, while a separate, explicit business-correlation attribute (a run id or workflow id) rides alongside as an ordinary CloudEvents extension attribute, carrying a domain-level identifier a trace ID alone does not (e.g. one that survives a re-fired trigger spanning multiple traces). The specification's own conflict rule -- general CloudEvents attribute serialization takes precedence over any secondary encoding the tracing extension defines -- is what keeps the two from silently disagreeing when both are present.
closures.standard: CloudEvents v1.0 distributed-tracing extension (CNCF) embedding W3C Trace Context (a W3C Recommendation); both are used together by design, not as alternatives.
closures.check: a schema check on emitted events asserting both a traceparent-carrying field and a distinct business-correlation attribute are present and non-empty on every event, with an equality assertion enforcing the spec's own precedence rule if the two encodings could otherwise disagree.
closures.direction: Settling: W3C Trace Context as the baseline propagation format, carried via the CloudEvents tracing extension, used concurrently with an explicit correlation attribute for business-level identity -- this is documented spec behavior, not an unresolved implementer choice. Nothing in the window is displacing this pairing.
closures.quote: the values of these two could differ by the time the event is received at a destination. In those cases, the serialization that followed the 'general CloudEvents serialization rules' MUST be used.

item.claim: How decision latency behaves when the input document must be assembled from remote state per call at agent scale.
item.research_query: policy decision point latency input document assembly remote data agent tool call rate 2026 benchmark production

closures.mechanism: Proposed, since no single benchmark sources it directly: a mature build keeps the policy decision itself in the sub-millisecond range by keeping remote-state fetches off the decision's hot path: the input document a policy evaluates is assembled from data that is pre-fetched, cached, or pushed via streaming bundle updates ahead of the call, so the measured evaluation latency (on the order of 0.2ms average, under 1ms p95 in published sidecar benchmarks) does not include a synchronous remote lookup. Where a decision genuinely needs fresh remote state, that fetch is budgeted and measured as a separate, named cost from evaluation, because no published benchmark found in the window reports the combined cost -- implying it is treated as a data-freshness/caching problem, not folded into the policy engine's own latency number.
closures.standard: none specific to this question; OPA and Cedar are the two live implementations (contested), with no shared standard for measuring or bounding remote-document-assembly latency.
closures.check: an end-to-end p95 decision-latency SLO measured at the tool-call gateway (not just engine-internal evaluation), reported as two distinct metrics -- policy evaluation time and input-document assembly time -- so a latency regression can be attributed to the right cause.
closures.direction: Settling: policy evaluation moving to the gateway boundary in front of every tool call (e.g. Cedar inside a major agent platform's policy service as of March 2026), with engine evaluation itself optimized into the sub-millisecond range. Still emerging/unsettled: a published benchmark that isolates remote-document-assembly cost from evaluation cost at agent tool-call rates.
closures.gap: no benchmark was found that isolates remote-document-assembly latency from policy-evaluation latency specifically; published figures (roughly 0.2ms average / under 1ms p95, or as low as 0.006-0.03ms in another measurement) report engine evaluation only, and separate agent-latency-budget research shows real multi-hop turns compounding 3-10x beyond single-call benchmarks without attributing that compounding to input assembly versus evaluation. Query used: "policy decision point latency input document assembly remote data agent tool call rate 2026 benchmark production".

item.claim: Whether a convention has emerged for carrying problem details over non-HTTP agent transports, so an agent-to-agent or event failure uses the same object rather than a transport-native error code.
item.research_query: RFC 9457 problem details over JSON-RPC gRPC messaging non-HTTP transport convention 2026 agent protocol error mapping

closures.mechanism: Proposed, extrapolating from an informal adaptation pattern rather than a ratified convention: a mature build reuses the RFC 9457 JSON object unchanged as the payload embedded in whatever error-carrying field the non-HTTP transport already provides -- for example packed as a typed value inside gRPC's `google.rpc.Status.details`, or as the `error.data` member of a JSON-RPC error response -- so the same problem-detail body (type, title, status, detail, instance, plus extension members) crosses transports, and only the outer envelope (HTTP status code vs. gRPC status code vs. JSON-RPC error code) differs by transport.
closures.standard: none -- RFC 9457 (RFC Editor, July 2023) is scoped to HTTP; no companion RFC, draft, or agent-protocol convention was found governing its use over JSON-RPC or gRPC specifically.
closures.check: a schema check that every non-HTTP error payload embeds a valid RFC 9457 object inside the transport's designated error-details field, validated against the same JSON Schema used to validate the HTTP path's problem+json bodies.
closures.direction: Emerging: ad hoc adaptation ("embed a similar structure in gRPC status details") is discussed at the blog/tutorial level, not standardized or adopted by any named agent protocol in the window. Abandoned: defining a wholly separate, transport-specific error shape per protocol rather than reusing the one problem-object schema.
closures.quote: The RFC 9457 model can be adapted for gRPC by embedding a similar structure in the gRPC status details, creating a single source of truth for all errors.
closures.gap: no ratified or de facto convention was found for carrying RFC 9457 over JSON-RPC or agent-to-agent transports specifically (A2A, MCP); only an informal, non-normative gRPC-embedding pattern surfaced, with no evidence of adoption by a named agent protocol. Query used: "RFC 9457 problem details over JSON-RPC gRPC messaging non-HTTP transport convention 2026 agent protocol error mapping".

item.claim: That revocation of an agent credential reliably halts work already in flight rather than only preventing new calls.
item.research_query: revoke short-lived agent credential in-flight task termination 2026 token revocation propagation latency

closures.mechanism: A mature build does not rely on a self-contained, offline-verifiable credential (a signed token nothing checks back against) for anything that must halt reliably mid-task, because such a token structurally cannot be revoked -- it can only be outlived. Instead it uses a broker-checked design where every action re-validates against a live revocation signal (an epoch, a revocation list, or introspection), accepting a bounded, measured propagation delay between the revoke call and 100% in-flight rejection (on the order of a few seconds in one production measurement using short polling and cache intervals), or a heartbeat-bound design where a delegated credential's validity is tied to periodic liveness proof from its issuer, so revocation is enforced by heartbeat cessation within a bounded window rather than a push notification that might not arrive.
closures.standard: none normative for the general case; OAuth 2.0 Token Introspection (RFC 7662) is the closest standard underpinning the broker-checked approach; heartbeat-bound credentialing is pre-standard research.
closures.check: a chaos test: revoke a credential mid-task and measure wall-clock time from the revoke call to the in-flight tool call actually being rejected; the build passes only if that time is bounded and the bound is published, not merely "eventually".
closures.direction: Settling: short-lived, broker-checked or introspected tokens over long-lived self-contained JWTs for anything needing mid-task revocation, with propagation delay treated as a measured, bounded, published number rather than assumed to be zero. Emerging: heartbeat-bound cryptographic revocation as a research direction (not yet production-standard) that would tighten the bound further. Abandoned: treating a signed, self-contained token as revocable at all.
closures.quote: Self-contained tokens cannot be revoked -- you can only outlive them.

item.claim: Whether the header draft was revived, replaced or formally abandoned after its April 2026 expiry - the search returned the expired revision but no later working-group action.
item.research_query: httpapi working group idempotency key header draft 08 status 2026 revived expired abandoned

closures.mechanism: Regardless of the header's own standardization status, a mature build implements idempotency as a de facto client-supplied key (the Stripe-popularized Idempotency-Key convention) checked at the application or gateway layer against a server-side dedup store keyed on the (key, request-fingerprint) pair, replaying the original result for a matching retry and rejecting a reused key with a different payload -- because production idempotency has never waited on IETF ratification to work.
closures.standard: draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header (IETF httpapi working group); latest version found is draft-07 (dated 2025-10-15, expiring 2026-04-18); no draft-08 or successor found, and no working-group action after expiry was located.
closures.check: a dedup-store test: replaying an identical Idempotency-Key plus payload digest within the store's retention window returns the original result without re-executing; a reused key with a differing payload digest is rejected (e.g. 409/422) rather than silently executed.
closures.direction: Settling: the de facto convention itself (application/gateway-layer dedup keyed on a client-supplied header) continues in production use regardless of IETF status. Unsettled inside the window: whether the IETF draft itself will be revived, replaced, or is being allowed to lapse permanently -- no working-group action after the April 2026 expiry was found in either direction.
closures.quote: The IETF draft has expired without becoming an RFC.
closures.gap: no evidence was found of httpapi working-group action (revival, replacement, or formal abandonment) after the draft's 2026-04-18 expiry; searches surfaced only draft-07 (dated 2025-10-15) and a third-party note that it "expired without becoming an RFC," with no draft-08 or successor document located. Query used: "httpapi working group idempotency key header draft 08 status 2026 revived expired abandoned".

item.claim: That a single read surface of record-by-identity, stream-from-version and projection is sufficient for cost planning over a typed dependency structure - this is my synthesis, not a sourced finding.
item.research_query: event sourced graph query surface projections planning cost estimation read model design 2026

closures.mechanism: Proposed, as this platform's own synthesis rather than a sourced sufficiency claim: the settled event-sourcing pattern derives every read surface -- a record fetched by identity, a stream replayed from a version, and a materialized projection for querying -- from the one append-only event log, treating the log as sole source of truth and every read surface as a regenerable view of it; production guidance names projection lag, projection failures, and event-log growth as the operational costs to plan for explicitly. Whether one such surface is *sufficient* for cost-planning purposes specifically over a typed dependency structure, as opposed to just being the standard read-model architecture, is this section's own synthesis and was not confirmed by any source found.
closures.standard: none named; CQRS plus Event Sourcing is a settled architectural pattern within its niche, not a ratified standard.
closures.check: a rebuild test: delete a projection and rebuild it from the log alone, asserting the result is byte-identical to the original; a cost dial (events replayed times average per-event processing time) predicts rebuild time within a measured tolerance, validating the log-as-source-of-truth assumption the sufficiency claim rests on.
closures.direction: Settling: read models/projections as the standard answer to query performance in event-sourced systems, with the log as sole write-side truth. Unsettled: no source ties this pattern to cost-planning sufficiency over a typed dependency structure specifically -- that remains this platform's inference, not an externally sourced claim.
closures.quote: Events are projected and stored in one or more read models, so they can be queried instead of the event streams.

item.question: Proposed question: For remote tool surfaces, which authorization and transport mechanisms are actually in force - the streamable transport rather than the deprecated event stream, OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, protected-resource and authorization-server metadata discovery, and resource indicators binding the token to one server on issue and on refresh?
item.target: Every mechanism is present and verified from the exchange itself, including the resource indicator on refresh, and tool results are validated against declared output schemas rather than read as prose.

closures.mechanism: A mature build treats every mechanism named in the question as independently verifiable from the wire exchange itself, not from configuration or documentation: the transport is Streamable HTTP (a single POST/SSE-upgrade endpoint, the deprecated HTTP+SSE transport retired); the client discovers the authorization server via RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata returned on a 401, and the authorization server via RFC 8414 metadata; the authorization code flow runs with PKCE (S256) as OAuth 2.1 requires for every client type; and every authorization request and every token request, including refresh, carries an RFC 8707 resource parameter naming the specific MCP server, so a token issued for one server is provably useless against another. Tool results are validated against the tool's declared output schema before being treated as structured data, rather than parsed out of prose.
closures.standard: Model Context Protocol Authorization specification, 2025-06-18 revision, built on OAuth 2.1 (IETF draft), RFC 9728 (Protected Resource Metadata), RFC 8414 (Authorization Server Metadata), RFC 8707 (Resource Indicators), and RFC 7636 (PKCE)
closures.check: A recorded token exchange transcript in which the authorization request, the initial token request, and every subsequent refresh request each carry the resource parameter, decoded token audience matches only the target server, and a captured attempt to replay the token against a second MCP server is rejected by that server; a schema-validation gate that rejects any tool result failing the tool's declared output schema.
closures.direction: Settling: OAuth 2.1 plus RFC 8707 resource indicators as the mandatory audience-binding mechanism for remote MCP servers, with Streamable HTTP fully replacing HTTP+SSE. Being abandoned: bearer tokens with no audience restriction, and treating tool output as free-form prose rather than schema-checked structured data. Still an open production gap rather than a settled abandonment: many real clients (including major ones) implement the resource parameter on the initial grant but omit it on refresh.
closures.quote: MCP clients MUST implement Resource Indicators as defined in RFC 8707 to explicitly specify the target resource, and the resource parameter MUST be included in both authorization requests and token requests, identifying the MCP server that the client intends to use the token with.

item.question: Does an allow have a stated scope and lifetime, so that work which was paused, queued, or resumed after a restart is decided again before its next side effect, or is a decision taken once treated as valid for as long as the run lasts? (This question is proposed, derived from the row it cites.)
item.target: A decision names the single action it admits and the moment it was taken; work resumed after a delay, a restart or a queue is decided again before its next side effect, and a rule changed in the interval takes effect on the resumed work.

closures.mechanism: A mature build stamps every allow decision with the single action it admits and the instant it was taken, and treats that decision as spent the moment its action either fires or is abandoned. Work that was paused, queued, or resumed after a restart carries no residual authorization: before its next side-effecting step it re-enters the decision point, which evaluates against the rule set and the principal's current state as they stand at resume time, not as they stood when the run was first admitted. A rule changed during the interval therefore takes effect on the resumed work without any special-casing, because there was never a cached decision to invalidate.
closures.standard: none — no single ratified standard governs decision lifetime; the mechanism is described in emerging runtime-governance reference architectures rather than a settled protocol
closures.check: A conformance run that admits a unit of work, changes the governing policy rule mid-run, forces a pause/queue/restart cycle, and then asserts the resumed work's next side-effecting call is denied (or altered) to match the new rule rather than the rule in force at original admission; the decision log shows two distinct decision records — pre-pause and post-resume — for the same run.
closures.direction: Emerging: pausing a queued or resumed side-effecting call for a fresh, parallel policy re-evaluation against current state, rather than trusting a decision made before the interruption. Being abandoned: session-scoped 'decide once, valid for the run' authorization, and silent credential/decision carry-over across a restart without an explicit owner decision.
closures.quote: Pause suspends the call until a parallel re-evaluation against the latest composite principal state completes.

item.evidence: .claude/skills/xc-correlation/SKILL.md: the guarantee names four planes (three signal kinds under four entry doors): "Bind all three emission kinds at once - spans, log records and problem objects - and count them separately in the audit rather than reporting one total." The stamp is set once at dis

closures.mechanism: A mature build binds all three emission kinds — spans, log records, and problem/error objects — to the same run identity at the moment each is produced, using the same trace and span identifiers, and counts and audits each kind separately rather than reporting one combined total that could hide a gap in one plane. The stamp is set once, at the entry that starts the unit of work, and every downstream span, log record, and problem object inherits it without a caller having to thread it through by hand.
closures.standard: OpenTelemetry Logs Data Model (stable specification), which defines TraceId, SpanId, and TraceFlags as top-level log-record fields
closures.check: For one run, assert that every span, every log record, and every emitted problem object carry an identical trace id, and that the audit counts each of the three kinds separately (three non-zero counters, not one), with a deliberately dropped stamp on one kind (e.g. a problem object built without the trace id) causing the check to fail.
closures.direction: Settling: OpenTelemetry's stable logs data model as the mechanism for span-to-log correlation, with several SDKs performing it automatically. Being abandoned: correlating by re-parsing free-text log lines for a run id, and treating error/problem objects as outside the correlation model entirely — this is the specific place current builds still fall short, since automatic correlation covers spans and logs but a problem object needs its own explicit stamp.
closures.quote: OpenTelemetry's stable log data model defines top-level TraceId, SpanId, and TraceFlags fields.

item.evidence: harness/idempotency/adapters/dryrun.py docstring: "which is the adapter-today row PASS.md B3 records for this element" naming (F-b3-16) "key on the wire, no lease", and "none. The conformance run's race case proves the gap: without a lock around" a claim-then-write. harness/idempotency/test.sh secti

closures.mechanism: A mature build never lets a caller's dedup key alone decide whether an operation is claimed; the claim and the write happen atomically (a single transaction or an explicit distributed lock), and the claim itself is a time-bounded lease rather than a permanent marker. A crash mid-operation leaves the lease to expire on its own TTL, so a retry after a real crash proceeds once the lease lapses, while a concurrent retry against a live lease is rejected outright — closing exactly the race a key-on-the-wire-with-no-lease design leaves open.
closures.standard: draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header-07 (IETF HTTPAPI working group, expires April 2026) for the header mechanics; lease semantics are established distributed-systems practice, not yet codified in that draft
closures.check: A race-case test that fires two concurrent requests carrying the same idempotency key against the same handler and asserts exactly one performs the side effect while the second is rejected or returns the first's result, plus a crash-recovery test that kills the process mid-write, waits past the lease TTL, and asserts the retried request is now allowed to proceed.
closures.direction: Settling: idempotency key plus a short-TTL processing lease, claimed atomically with the write, as the production pattern for retry-safe side effects. Being abandoned: recording a key on the wire with no server-side lock or lease, which is exactly the gap this repo's dry-run adapter still has, per its own docstring.
closures.quote: A lease allows recovery after a crash... your idempotency key should have a processing-phase TTL that is short enough to expire before the client's retry window closes.

item.claim: That the runtime specification itself defines pause, resume, snapshot or fork as standard lifecycle operations, rather than these being adapter-specific extensions.
item.research_query: OCI runtime specification lifecycle operations pause resume checkpoint restore standardisation status

closures.mechanism: A mature build treats pause, resume, snapshot, and fork as capabilities layered on top of the runtime specification's base lifecycle (create, start, kill, delete plus hooks) rather than as operations the specification itself standardizes. The core imports only the OCI runtime-spec's create/start/delete contract; a checkpoint/restore or snapshot/fork capability is provided by a specific adapter (a CRIU-backed runtime, or a platform-specific sandbox API) behind a capability interface, so swapping that adapter never changes what the core is entitled to assume.
closures.standard: OCI Runtime Specification (opencontainers/runtime-spec, current release), which does not define checkpoint/restore, pause, snapshot, or fork as base lifecycle states
closures.check: A schema or interface-conformance check that the core only calls the four base lifecycle verbs (create, start, kill/pause-signal, delete) against the runtime-spec interface, plus a second-adapter test proving pause/resume/snapshot/fork can be swapped (e.g. a CRIU-backed runc versus a platform sandbox snapshot API) without a core code change.
closures.direction: Emerging: a dedicated Checkpoint/Restore Working Group (announced January 2026, tied to CRIU and Kubernetes) standardizing checkpoint/restore practice outside the base runtime-spec, while individual runtimes (runc, crun) add CRIU-backed support opportunistically. Being abandoned: waiting for the OCI runtime-spec itself to absorb these as base lifecycle verbs — the direction is a companion working group and runtime-level opt-in, not a runtime-spec revision.
closures.quote: The OCI Runtime Specification defines standard container lifecycle phases including creating, created, running, and deleted states with associated hooks.

item.claim: Whether hard budget termination at the model boundary is a common production practice or mostly a documented feature.
item.research_query: production evidence enforced token budget termination LLM gateway 2026 case studies measured

closures.mechanism: A mature build enforces a token/spend ceiling at the gateway itself, as a policy the execution infrastructure evaluates and acts on, not as a metric that triggers a human-facing alert. When a session or call crosses its ceiling, the gateway terminates the in-flight request or session immediately, with no human confirmation required to stop the spend, and the termination is itself an auditable event.

closures.direction: Settling: hard, policy-evaluated termination at the gateway as the answer to a well-documented failure class (63 catalogued production budget-overrun incidents across 21 frameworks). Being abandoned: budget tracking as an alerting-only, human-in-the-loop dashboard metric with no automatic stop.
closures.quote: When the ceiling is hit, the session stops — not because someone responded to an alert, but because the execution infrastructure evaluated a policy and terminated the session, with no human in the loop required at the cost enforcement layer.
closures.gap: What proportion of production LLM gateway deployments actually wire hard termination versus alert-only budgets was not measured by any source found; query used: "production evidence enforced token budget termination LLM gateway 2026 case studies measured".

item.claim: Whether the protocol itself defines a non-interactive or policy-answered permission mode, as opposed to implementations adding one.

closures.mechanism: A mature build treats session/request_permission (or the protocol's equivalent) as the one interactive permission method the protocol defines, and implements non-interactive operation as a client-side policy layer that answers that same method automatically — matching each request against a local allow/deny rule set, a hook, or a headless timeout — rather than inventing a second, protocol-blessed 'non-interactive mode'. A client that skips the method entirely to auto-approve is deviating from the spec, not exercising a documented mode of it.

closures.direction: Settling: request_permission as the universal handshake, with headless/CI clients answering it via a local policy engine (allow-list, hooks) rather than a human prompt. Being abandoned: clients that bypass the handshake altogether in headless mode, which several current implementations (including a major CLI) are documented as doing incorrectly.

item.claim: What operators running hundreds of concurrent agents actually use for work intake at scale, and whether they normalise the four doors into one envelope or keep them separate.
item.research_query: production multi-agent platform 2026 architecture hundreds of agents work intake normalisation CloudEvents A2A case study

closures.mechanism: A mature build normalizes every entry door — a human request, an inbound event, a schedule firing, and an inter-agent task delegated over an agent-to-agent protocol — into one canonical work envelope before any downstream component sees it, so a downstream planner or graph never branches on which door the work arrived through. The agent-to-agent leg of that intake increasingly runs over a settling inter-agent protocol rather than a bespoke integration per platform pair.

closures.check: A schema check that a human-submitted request, a webhook-delivered event, a scheduler firing, and an inbound A2A task all produce structurally identical envelope documents (same required fields, same shape) before entering the planner, with a test that a downstream consumer's logic path is provably identical across all four origins.

Emerging and unsettled: whether operators normalize A2A tasks together with the other three doors into one canonical envelope, or keep A2A as a separate lane — no source inside the window documents the practice at hundreds-of-agents scale either way.

item.claim: How large agent platforms validate documents whose shape is only known at run time, where a schema must be resolved per unit of work rather than compiled once.
item.research_query: dynamic schema resolution per request agent tool input validation 2026 compile cache JSON Schema performance production

closures.mechanism: A mature build never recompiles a schema on the hot path. Whatever a unit of work's declared shape is at run time, the validator resolves it through a compiled-schema cache keyed by schema identity (a URI, hash, or version), compiling once on first sight and reusing the compiled validator on every subsequent unit that declares the same shape — even when the specific schema in play could only be known once the unit of work arrived.
closures.standard: JSON Schema (2020-12 dialect), with per-implementation compiled-validator caching as established practice rather than something the specification itself mandates
closures.check: A benchmark that submits a stream of units of work spanning a fixed set of schemas in random order and asserts p99 validation latency after warm-up is within a small constant factor of a pre-compiled baseline (not proportional to the number of distinct schemas seen), with a cache-hit counter confirming repeated schemas are not recompiled.
closures.direction: Settling: compile-once, cache, and reuse the compiled validator, keyed by schema identity — resolving 'the schema is only known at run time' by resolving identity at run time and compilation at most once per identity. Being abandoned: recompiling a schema on every request, and heavy use of fully dynamic ($dynamicRef-style) schema resolution, which surveyed corpora show is rare in practice.
closures.quote: Avoiding per-request schema compilation can yield a 1000× performance difference by compiling once per schema and reusing the validator.

item.claim: Whether the published decision API's request shape can express a budget ceiling and a delegation chain without extensions, or whether those require profile-specific fields.

closures.mechanism: A mature build issues the published decision API's request as-is for the ordinary case — subject, action, resource, and context, each an open type/id/properties triple — and reaches for a named profile extension, not ad-hoc fields, whenever it needs to express something the base request shape does not: a delegation chain (an actor distinct from subject) or a spend ceiling ride in the properties bag until or unless a dedicated profile standardizes them, at which point the build adopts that profile rather than inventing its own field names.
closures.standard: AuthZEN Authorization API 1.0 (OpenID Foundation, Final Specification since January 2026); delegation and agent-tool concerns are addressed by separate Working Group Drafts (AARP — Access Request and Approval Profile; COAZ — MCP Tool Authorization Profile)
closures.check: A schema-conformance test that a request expressing a delegation chain or a budget ceiling validates against the base AuthZEN 1.0 schema only by using the open 'properties' object (never a top-level extension the base spec doesn't define), and a second test that a profile-aware PDP recognizes and enforces those properties when the relevant profile is declared.
closures.direction: Settling: AuthZEN 1.0's subject/action/resource/context shape as the baseline, with delegation and agent-specific semantics being added through dedicated profile drafts published in 2026 rather than through base-schema extension fields. Being abandoned: bespoke, PDP-specific request shapes for delegation or budget that don't map onto AuthZEN's open properties model.
closures.quote: A Subject is an object that contains two REQUIRED keys, type and id, which have a string value, and an OPTIONAL key, properties, with a value of an object.

Emerging and unmeasured inside the window: what to attest fully versus hash-only at hundreds-of-agents action rates — the cost/retention tradeoff research found (metadata-light recovery, pre-execution mediation overhead) is early and not yet benchmarked at that scale.

item.claim: That an attested workload identity plane and an assertion-grant issuer can satisfy one identity interface without the interface leaking either token shape - asserted from the two mechanisms separately, not from a source describing both behind one abstraction.
item.research_query: single workload identity abstraction over SPIFFE JWT-SVID and OAuth token exchange interface design 2026 pluggable issuer

closures.mechanism: A mature build exposes one identity interface to its core, but behind that interface it composes two genuinely separate mechanisms rather than blending them: a SPIFFE/SPIRE-issued JWT-SVID asserts which workload is calling (short-lived, auto-rotated, verifiable against a trust bundle), and a token-exchange step at an authorization server converts that workload assertion into an OAuth access token scoped to what the workload may do. The interface's contract names both steps explicitly rather than describing a single fused token shape, so a caller can swap either the SPIFFE issuer or the OAuth authorization server independently.

closures.check: A two-adapter test that swaps the SPIFFE issuer (e.g. two different SPIRE deployments) and separately swaps the OAuth authorization server, asserting the interface's callers need no code change either time, plus an assertion that the interface's documented contract never leaks a raw JWT-SVID where an OAuth access token is expected or vice versa.
closures.direction: Emerging: composing WIMSE, SPIFFE, and OAuth token exchange as a layered identity model, formalized in early-2026 IETF drafts (AIMS) but not yet a ratified single interface. Being abandoned: shared, long-lived OAuth client-credential secrets for workload identity in favor of short-lived, auto-rotated SPIFFE SVIDs exchanged per-call.
closures.quote: SPIFFE provides workload identity in cloud-native environments via X.509 or JWT SVIDs, with production deployments at Uber, Stripe, and Netflix.

item.claim: That inclusion and consistency proofs are practical at the write rate a busy agent platform generates, rather than at certificate-issuance rates.

closures.mechanism: A mature build treats an inclusion or consistency proof as a cheap, constant-work-per-query operation (logarithmic in log size, sub-kilobyte proof size) and generates one for any entry a caller needs to verify without holding the whole log, at the platform's actual write rate — which recent Merkle-log implementations demonstrate comfortably exceeds typical agent-platform action rates, so this is an engineering choice to make, not a scalability wall to work around.
